extracted_passages.normalized_text: Commentators have noted the different uses Tolkien made of trolls, from comedy in Sam Gamgee's poem and the Cockney accents and table manners of the working-class trolls in The Hobbit, to the hellish atmosphere in Moria as the protagonists are confronted by darkness and monsters. Tolkien, a Roman Catholic, drew back from giving trolls the power of speech, as he had done in The Hobbit, as it implied to him that they had souls and thereby confronting him with a moral dilemma, so he made the trolls in The Silmarillion and The Lord of the Rings darker and more bestial. They were supposedly bred by the Dark Lords Melkor and Sauron for their own evil purposes in mockery of ents, helping to express Tolkien's combination of "fairy tale with epic, ... bonded with the Christian mythos".
thumb|In Norse mythology, the god Thor talked to the dwarf Alviss to prevent him from marrying his daughter Þrúðr; at dawn Alviss turns to stone. Drawing by W. G. Collingwood, 1908

Christina Fawcett, a scholar of English, writes that Tolkien synthesises materials from different eras, so his writing and his creatures can take on different qualities, from playful to monstrous; his hill-trolls "while still threatening, are primarily comic and slow-witted". On the other hand, when Gandalf outwits them, these same trolls are seen as "monstrous, a warning against vice, captured forever in stone for their greed and anger." All the same, Fawcett cautions that Tolkien uses tradition selectively, transferring the more positive attributes of Norse trolls, including being rich and generous, to hobbits.
thumb|upright=0.9|Tolkien based details such as the trolls' tiredness with mutton on William Morris's travels in Iceland. Drawing of Morris cooking in Iceland c. 1870 by Edward Burne-Jones
thumb|upright|Tolkien's wordless trolls have been compared to Grendel, a monster in Beowulf. Illustration by J. R. Skelton, 1908

Fawcett suggests that Tolkien's "roaring Troll" in The Return of the King reflects the Beowulf monster Grendel's "[fiery] eye and terrible screaming." Noting that Tolkien compares them to beasts as they "came striding up, roaring like beasts ... bellowing", she observes that they "remain wordless warriors, like Grendel", although they are sentient, with intelligence and a single language, unlike the varied tongues of Tolkien's orcs.

Critics including Fawcett and Hartley note that by making all the beasts in The Hobbit talk, Tolkien, a devout Roman Catholic, had created a serious problem for himself: if trolls and other monsters were supposed to be sentient, they would in Christian terms have souls and be redeemable rather than wholly evil. Tolkien acknowledged this keenly-felt question: "Of course ... when you make Trolls speak [Tolkien's emphasis] you are giving them a power, which in our world (probably) connotes the possession of a 'soul'." Fawcett distinguishes the approach of Tolkien's narrator, who treats trolls as "wholly monstrous", from his "translator's notes" which take "a slightly more balanced view". She states that Tolkien adopts a similar multiplicity of viewpoints on the in-fiction creation of trolls: Frodo tells Sam that the Shadow cannot create "real new things of its own", but all the same, she writes, the "stone-bred mockery" seems very much alive. This is, Fawcett writes, in contrast to Tolkien's intelligent dragons, which are straightforwardly a created species with the power of speech, but certainly monsters; and in contrast to orcs which, if they are corrupted elves, do have souls. She concludes that Tolkien's linking of souls to speech "complicates these monstrous races".

William Huggins }} '''Trolls''' are fictional characters in [[J. R. R. Tolkien]]'s [[Middle-earth]], and feature in films and games adapted from his novels. They are portrayed as [[Tolkien's monsters|monstrously]] large humanoids of great strength and poor intellect. In ''[[The Hobbit]]'', like the dwarf [[Alviss]] of [[Norse mythology]], they must be below ground before dawn or turn to stone, whereas in ''[[The Lord of the Rings]]'' they are able to face daylight. Commentators have noted the different uses Tolkien made of trolls, from comedy in [[Sam Gamgee]]'s poem and the [[Cockney]] accents and [[table manners]] of the [[working-class]] trolls in ''The Hobbit'', to the [[hell]]ish atmosphere in [[Moria (Middle-earth)|Moria]] as the protagonists are confronted by darkness and monsters. Tolkien, a [[Roman Catholic]], drew back from giving trolls the power of speech, as he had done in ''The Hobbit'', as it implied to him that they had [[soul]]s and thereby confronting him with [[Tolkien's moral dilemma|a moral dilemma]], so he made the trolls in ''[[The Silmarillion]]'' and ''The Lord of the Rings'' darker and more bestial. They were supposedly bred by the Dark Lords [[Melkor]] and [[Sauron]] for their own evil purposes in mockery of ents, helping to express Tolkien's combination of "fairy tale with epic, ... bonded with the Christian mythos". == Appearances == ===''The Hobbit''=== {{Quote box |quote="Mutton yesterday, mutton today, and blimey, if it don't look like mutton again tomorrer", said one of the trolls. "Never a blinking bit of manflesh have we had for long enough", said a second. |source=— from "Roast Mutton" in ''[[The Hobbit]]'' |width=40% |align=right }} In ''[[The Hobbit]]'', [[Bilbo Baggins]] and the [[Dwarf (Middle-earth)|Dwarf]] company encountered three stone trolls on their journey to [[Erebor]]. The stone trolls captured the Dwarves and prepared to eat them, but the [[Wizard (Middle-Earth)|wizard]] [[Gandalf]] managed to distract them until dawn, when exposure to sunlight turned them to stone. They had vulgar [[table manners]], constantly argued and fought amongst themselves, in Tolkien's narrator's words "not [[drawing-room]] fashion at all, at all", spoke with [[Cockney]] accents, and had matching English working-class names: Tom, Bert, and William.{{harvnb|Tolkien|1937}}, ch. 2 "Roast Mutton"{{cite book |last1=Stevens |first1=David |last2=Stevens |first2=Carol D. |title=J. R. R. Tolkien |chapter=The Hobbit |editor-first1=Harold |editor-last1=Bloom |series=Bloom's Modern Critical Views |publisher=Bloom's Literary Criticism |year=2008 |isbn=978-1-60413-146-8 |pages=17–26 }} Jennifer Eastman Attebery, a scholar of English, states that the stone trolls in ''The Hobbit'' "signify the [[wikt:uncouth|uncouth]]".{{cite journal |last=Attebery |first=Jennifer Eastman |title=The Trolls of Fiction: Ogres or Warm Fuzzies? |journal=[[Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts]] |date=1996 |volume=7 |issue=1 (25) |pages=61–74 |jstor=43308256 |quote=The comedy is conveyed chiefly through the trolls' lower class British dialect and their clumsy handling of little Bilbo}} ===''The Lord of the Rings''=== {{Quote box |quote='My lad,' said Troll, 'this bone I stole.
But what be bones that lie in a hole?
Thy nuncle was dead as a lump o' lead,
Afore I found his shinbone.
Tinbone! Skinbone!
He can spare a share for a poor old troll,
For he don't need his shinbone.' |source=—from "The Stone Troll" in ''[[The Fellowship of the Ring]]'' |width=40% |align=right }} As Aragorn and the four hobbit companions made their way towards [[Rivendell]] through the Trollshaws, they came upon the three trolls that Bilbo and the dwarves had encountered many years earlier, and had seen turned to stone at daybreak. [[Sam Gamgee]] recited a [[comic poem]], "The Stone Troll", on the supposed dangers of kicking a troll, who has a "seat" which is "harder than stone", to cheer everyone up.{{harvnb|Tolkien|1954a}}, book 1, ch. 12, "Flight to the Ford" {{Quote box |quote=Olog-hai they were called in the Black Speech. That Sauron bred them none doubted, though from what stock was not known... Trolls they were, but filled with the evil will of their master: a fell race, strong, agile, fierce and cunning, but harder than stone. Unlike the older race of the Twilight they could endure the Sun, so long as the will of Sauron held sway over them. They spoke little, and the only tongue that they knew was the Black Speech of Barad-dûr. |source=Tolkien's description of the trolls in Appendix F "Of Other Races" in ''[[The Return of the King]]''{{harvnb|Tolkien|1955}} Appendix F "Of Other Races" |width=40% |align=right }} Cave trolls attacked the Fellowship in [[Moria (Middle-earth)|Moria]]. One had dark greenish scales, black blood, and a hide so thick that when [[Boromir]] struck it in the arm his sword was notched. However, Frodo was able to impale the "toeless" foot of the same troll with the enchanted dagger [[Sting (Middle-earth)|Sting]].{{harvnb|Tolkien|1954a}}, book 2, ch. 5 "The Bridge of Khazad-dûm" Mountain trolls wielded the great [[battering ram]] [[List of Middle-earth weapons and armour#Grond|Grond]] to shatter the gates of [[Minas Tirith]].{{harvnb|Tolkien|1955}}, book 5, ch. 4 "The Siege of Gondor" They fought using clubs and round shields at the [[Battle of the Morannon]].{{harvnb|Tolkien|1955}}, book 5, ch. 10, "The Black Gate Opens"{{cite book |last=Krege |first=Wolfgang |author-link=Wolfgang Krege |title=Handbuch der Weisen von Mittelerde |language=de |trans-title=Handbook of the Sages of Middle-earth |date=1999 |publisher={{ill|Klett-Cotta Verlag|de}} |isbn=3-608-93521-5 |pages=348–349}} Sauron bred mountain and cave trolls, and developed the more intelligent Olog-hai that were not vulnerable to sunlight.{{cite thesis |last=Fawcett |first=Christina |title=J.R.R. Tolkien and the morality of monstrosity |date=February 2014 |publisher=[[University of Glasgow]] (PhD thesis) |url=http://theses.gla.ac.uk/4993/ |pages=29, 97, 125-131|type=PhD }} Snow trolls are mentioned only in the story of [[Helm Hammerhand]]. When Helm went out during the Long Winter clad in white to ambush his enemies, he was described as looking like a snow-troll.{{harvnb|Tolkien|1955}}, Appendix A. II "The House of Eorl" {{anchor|Trollshaws}} The Trollshaws is a wooded region, lying north of the East Road between the rivers [[Hoarwell]] and [[Bruinen]], where Bilbo encountered the trolls. It is not named in the text of either ''The Hobbit'' or ''The Lord of the Rings'', but appears on the latter's [[Tolkien's maps|map of Middle-earth]] drawn by [[Christopher Tolkien]]. Described as "the Trolls' wood" in the main text, the name "Trollshaws" is derived from ''troll'' + ''shaw'', an archaic term for a thicket or small wood.{{cite book |last1=Hammond |first1=Wayne G. |author-link=Wayne G. Hammond |last2=Scull |first2=Christina |author2-link=Christina Scull |title=The Lord of the Rings: A Reader's Companion |year=2005 |publisher=[[Houghton Mifflin Harcourt|Houghton Mifflin]] |isbn=978-0-00-720907-1 |title-link=The Lord of the Rings: A Reader's Companion |page=lxiii }} ===''The Silmarillion''=== {{Quote box |quote=Last of all [[Húrin]] stood alone. Then he cast aside his shield, and wielded an axe two-handed; and it is sung that the axe smoked in the black blood of the troll-guard of [[Gothmog]] until it withered... |source=—from "Nirnaeth Arnoediad" in ''[[The Silmarillion]]''{{harvnb|Tolkien|1977}}, ch. 20 "Of the Fifth Battle: Nirnaeth Arnoediad", p. 195 |width=40% |align=right }} [[Morgoth]], the evil [[Vala (Middle-earth)|Vala]], created trolls in the [[First Age]] of [[Middle-earth]].{{harvnb|Tolkien|1955}} Appendix F, "The Languages and Peoples of the Third Age", "Of Other Races" They were strong and vicious but stupid; as in ''The Hobbit'', they turned to stone in sunlight. During the wars of [[Beleriand]], [[Gothmog]] (the Lord of [[Balrogs]]) had a bodyguard of trolls. During the [[Nírnaeth Arnoediad]], the Battle of Unnumbered Tears, in which Morgoth defeated the united armies of Elves, Men, and Dwarves, the great warrior [[Húrin]], a [[Man (Middle-earth)|Man]], faced Gothmog's trolls to protect the retreat of the Elven king Turgon. Morgoth's order to Gothmog to capture Húrin alive allowed Húrin to kill all the trolls. Many trolls died in the [[War of Wrath]], but some survived and joined [[Sauron]], the greatest surviving servant of Morgoth.{{harvnb|Tolkien|2007}}, ch. 2 "The Battle of Unnumbered Tears"{{harvnb|Tolkien|1977}}, ch. 20 "Of the Fifth Battle: Nirnaeth Arnoediad", p. 195 == Origins == {{further|Tolkien and the Norse}} [[File:All-wise answers Thor.jpg|thumb|In [[Norse mythology]], the god [[Thor]] talked to the [[Dwarf (folklore)|dwarf]] [[Alviss]] to prevent him from marrying his daughter [[Þrúðr]]; at dawn Alviss turns to stone. Drawing by [[W. G. Collingwood]], 1908]] In [[Germanic mythology]], [[troll]]s are a kind of giant, along with ''rísar'', ''[[jötunn|jötnar]]'', and ''þursar''; the names are variously applied to large monstrous beings, sometimes as synonyms.{{cite book |last=Simek |first=Rudolf |author-link=Rudolf Simek |chapter=Trolle (trolls) |title=Mittelerde: Tolkien und die germanische Mythologie |trans-title=Middle-earth: Tolkien and Germanic Mythology |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1Hubdk3wZuMC |year=2005 |publisher=C. H. Beck |language=de |isbn=978-3-406-52837-8 |pages=124–128}}{{cite book | last=Orchard | first=Andy | title=Dictionary of Norse myth and legend | publisher=[[Cassell (publisher)|Cassell]] | year=1997 | isbn=978-0304345205 | page=197}} The idea that such monsters must be below ground before dawn dates back to the ''[[Elder Edda]]'' of [[Norse mythology]], where in the [[Alvíssmál]], the god [[Thor]] keeps the dwarf [[Alviss]] (not a troll) talking until dawn, and sees him turn to stone.{{cite book |last=Shippey |first=Tom |author-link=Tom Shippey |title=[[The Road to Middle-Earth]] |date=1982 |publisher=Grafton ([[HarperCollins]]) |isbn=0261102753 |page=69}}{{cite book |last=Burns |first=Marjorie |author-link=Marjorie Burns |year=2007 |chapter=Old Norse literature |title=[[J.R.R. Tolkien Encyclopedia]] |editor=Drout, Michael D. C. |publisher=[[Routledge]] |pages=473–479 |isbn=978-0-41596-942-0}}{{cite book |last=Shippey |first=Tom |author-link=Tom Shippey |title=[[J. R. R. Tolkien: Author of the Century]] |date=2001 |publisher=HarperCollins |isbn=978-0261-10401-3 |pages=12, 19–20}} [[Tom Shippey]], a Tolkien scholar, writes that ''The Hobbit''{{'s}} audience in 1937 were familiar with trolls from [[fairy tale]] collections such as [[Grimms' Fairy Tales|those of Grimm]], and [[Asbjørnsen and Moe]]'s ''[[Norwegian Folktales]]''; Tolkien's use of monsters of different kinds – orcs, trolls, and a [[balrog]] in [[Moria (Middle-earth)|Moria]] – made that journey "a descent into [[hell]]". Attebery writes that Trolls thus moved from being grim Norse ogres to more sympathetic modern humanoids. In her view, Tolkien's trolls are based on the ogre type, but with two "incarnations": ancient trolls, "creatures of dull and lumpish nature" in Tolkien's words,{{harvnb|Tolkien|1955}}, Appendix F, I, "Of Other Races", "Trolls" unable to speak; and the malicious giants of strength and courage bred by Sauron with "enough intelligence to present a real danger". The scholar of English Edward Risden agrees that Tolkien's later trolls appear far more dangerous than those of ''The Hobbit'', losing, too, "the [moral] capacity to relent"; he comments that in Norse mythology, trolls are "normally female and strongly associated with magic", while in the Norse sagas the trolls were physically strong and superhuman in battle.{{cite book |last=Risden |first=Edward L. |title=Tolkien's Intellectual Landscape |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5YP2BgAAQBAJ&pg=PA141 |year=2015 |publisher=[[McFarland & Company|McFarland]] |isbn=978-0-7864-9865-9 |page=141}} Christina Fawcett, a scholar of English, writes that Tolkien synthesises [[Anachronism in Middle-earth|materials from different eras]], so his writing and his creatures can take on different qualities, from playful to monstrous; his hill-trolls "while still threatening, are primarily comic and slow-witted". On the other hand, when Gandalf outwits them, these same trolls are seen as "monstrous, a warning against vice, captured forever in stone for their greed and anger." All the same, Fawcett cautions that Tolkien uses tradition selectively, transferring the more positive attributes of Norse trolls, including being rich and generous, to [[hobbit]]s. == Analysis == === Trolls in ''The Hobbit'' === [[File:William Morris cooking in Iceland by Edward Burne-Jones.jpg|thumb|upright=0.9|Tolkien based details such as the trolls' tiredness with [[mutton]] on [[William Morris]]'s travels in Iceland. Drawing of Morris cooking in Iceland c. 1870 by [[Edward Burne-Jones]]]] Shippey criticises Tolkien's [[Class (social)|class]]-based depiction of the trolls and goblins in ''The Hobbit'', writing that the trolls were too close to labourers, just as the goblins were to [[ammunition|munitions workers]]. Shippey notes, too, Tolkien's storytelling technique here, observing that making the troll's purse (which Bilbo attempts to steal) able to speak blurs the line between the ordinary and the magical.{{cite book |last=Shippey |first=Tom |author-link=Tom Shippey |title=[[The Road to Middle-Earth]] |date=2005 |edition=Third |orig-year=1982 |publisher=[[HarperCollins]] |isbn=978-0261102750 |pages=85–87}} [[Marjorie Burns]], a scholar of English literature, writes that the trolls' tiredness with eating [[mutton]] every day matches the fantasy writer and designer [[William Morris]]'s account of his travels in [[Iceland]] in the early 1870s, one of many Middle-earth features that follows Morris, including the existence of trolls: Morris mentioned visiting places called ''Tröllakirkja'' ("Trollchurch") and ''Tröllahals'' ("Trollneck"). Burns notes, too, that the adventure with the three trolls combines Bilbo's fear of being eaten with the temptation of the "fine toothsome smell" of roast mutton.{{cite book |last=Burns |first=Marjorie |author-link=Marjorie Burns |title=Perilous Realms: Celtic and Norse in Tolkien's Middle-earth |title-link=Perilous Realms |year=2005 |publisher=[[University of Toronto Press]] |isbn=978-0-8020-3806-7 |pages=84, 159–161}} The critic Gregory Hartley notes that while in ''The Hobbit'', Tolkien's trolls were still much like those of Norse mythology, "archetypal, stereotypical ... basking in unexamined sentience",{{cite book |last=Hartley |first=Gregory |chapter=Civilized goblins and Talking Animals: How The Hobbit Created Problems of Sentience for Tolkien |editor=[[Bradford Lee Eden]] |title=The Hobbit and Tolkien's mythology : essays on revisions and influences |publisher=[[McFarland & Company|McFarland]] |year=2014 |isbn=978-0-7864-7960-3 |oclc=889426663 |volume=Part III: Themes }} in ''The Silmarillion'' and ''Lord of the Rings'', "Tolkien undertook the difficult task of melding [[fairy tale]] with [[Epic fantasy|epic]], which was in turn bonded with the Christian mythos. Characters and creatures began functioning on a multiplicity of registers." The entertainingly "light-hearted informality" of ''The Hobbit''{{'}}s Cockney-speaking trolls thus gave way to the "more bestial trolls" of the later works. Hartley comments that the [[Redaction (editorial synthesis)|redaction]] effort that Tolkien threw himself into for his legendarium was driven by the way he had composed ''The Hobbit''; and that the resulting "rich, curious roles" that trolls and other beasts play in Middle-earth would not have existed without it. === Speech, sentience, and souls === {{main|Tolkien's moral dilemma}} [[File:Stories of beowulf grendel.jpg|thumb|upright|Tolkien's wordless trolls have been compared to [[Grendel]], a monster in ''[[Beowulf]]''. Illustration by [[Joseph Ratcliffe Skelton|J. R. Skelton]], 1908]] Fawcett suggests that Tolkien's "roaring Troll" in ''[[The Return of the King]]'' reflects the [[Beowulf]] monster [[Grendel]]'s "[fiery] eye and terrible screaming." Noting that Tolkien compares them to beasts as they "came striding up, roaring like beasts ... bellowing", she observes that they "remain wordless warriors, like Grendel", although they are sentient, with intelligence and a single language, unlike the varied tongues of Tolkien's orcs. Critics including Fawcett and Hartley note that by making all the beasts in ''The Hobbit'' talk, Tolkien, a devout [[Roman Catholic]], had created a serious problem for himself: if trolls and other monsters were supposed to be sentient, they would in Christian terms have [[Soul#Christianity|souls]] and be redeemable rather than wholly [[Evil in Middle-earth|evil]]. Tolkien acknowledged this keenly-felt question: "Of course ... when you make Trolls ''speak'' [Tolkien's emphasis] you are giving them a power, which in our world (probably) connotes the possession of a 'soul'." Fawcett distinguishes the approach of Tolkien's narrator, who treats trolls as "wholly monstrous", from his "translator's notes" which take "a slightly more balanced view". She states that Tolkien adopts a similar multiplicity of viewpoints on the in-fiction creation of trolls: Frodo tells Sam that the Shadow cannot create "real new things of its own", but all the same, she writes, the "stone-bred mockery" seems very much alive. This is, Fawcett writes, in contrast to Tolkien's intelligent [[Dragon (Middle-earth)|dragons]], which are straightforwardly a created species with the power of speech, but certainly monsters; and in contrast to orcs which, if they are corrupted elves, do have souls. She concludes that Tolkien's linking of souls to speech "complicates these monstrous races". Tolkien had another conceptual problem with the existence of evil creatures, as he believed that while good could create, evil could not. So he considered whether his evil creatures could have been corrupted from sentient beings, and whether they could breed, writing various and contradictory explanations of their origins.{{cite book |last=Shippey |first=Tom |author-link=Tom Shippey |title=[[J. R. R. Tolkien: Author of the Century]] |date=2001 |publisher=[[HarperCollins]] |isbn=978-0261-10401-3 |page=265}} In ''The Two Towers'', the leader of the [[Ent]]s, [[Treebeard]], remarks that trolls were "made ... in mockery of Ents", as [[Orc (Middle-earth)|Orcs]] were of [[Elf (Middle-earth)|Elves]].{{harvnb|Tolkien|1954}}, book 3, ch. 4, "Treebeard"{{cite book |last1=Hammond |first1=Wayne G. |author1-link=Wayne G. Hammond |last2=Scull |first2=Christina |author2-link=Christina Scull |title=The Lord of the Rings: A Reader's Companion |title-link=The Lord of the Rings: A Reader's Companion |publisher=[[HarperCollins]] | year=2005 |isbn=978-0-00-720907-1 |pages=76, 389}}{{harvnb|Carpenter|2023|loc=#153, to Peter Hastings, September 1954. }} Friedhelm Schneidewind, writing in the ''[[J. R. R. Tolkien Encyclopedia]]'', states the precise origin of trolls "perhaps from giant apes but possibly from Men, Orcs, or 'Spirits'" is not given by Tolkien, but like Orcs, trolls were bred by [[Melkor]] and Sauron for their own evil purposes.{{cite encyclopedia |last=Schneidewind |first=Friedhelm |editor-last=Drout |editor-first=Michael D. C. |editor-link=Michael D. C. Drout |title=Biology of Middle-earth |encyclopedia=[[J.R.R. Tolkien Encyclopedia|J.R.R. Tolkien Encyclopedia: Scholarship and Critical Assessment]] |year=2013 |orig-year=2007 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-0-415-86511-1 |page=66}} === Defeat of evil === The Inklings scholar [[Charles A. Huttar]] writes that the trolls' presence, alongside [[orc]]s and the [[Balrog]], means that "Moria not only houses inert obstacles but active monsters".{{cite book |last=Huttar |first=Charles A. |author-link=Charles A. Huttar |editor-last=Lobdell |editor-first=Jared |editor-link=Jared Lobdell |chapter=Hell and The City: Tolkien and the Traditions of Western Literature |title=[[A Tolkien Compass]] |date=1975 |publisher=[[Open Court Publishing Company|Open Court]] |isbn=978-0-87548-303-0 |page=125}} Burns notes that with the destruction of Sauron, trolls, like the rest of Sauron's minions, were scattered in defeat, though some survived by hiding in the hills. In Burns's view, this makes Tolkien appear both optimistic, since evil can be defeated, and pessimistic, as that defeat is never absolute.{{cite book |last=Burns |first=Marjorie |author-link=Marjorie Burns |title=Perilous Realms: Celtic and Norse in Tolkien's Middle-earth |year=2005 |publisher=[[University of Toronto Press]] |isbn=978-0-8020-3806-7 |page=176}} === Country folk music === {{further|Music in Middle-earth}} The Tolkien scholar [[David Bratman]] writes that even though there is no [[sheet music]] in Tolkien's Middle-earth writings, we do "surprisingly" have "a very good idea" of how some of it should sound. In 1952, Tolkien recited part of ''The Lord of the Rings'' for [[George Sayer (biographer)|George Sayer]] to record, and sang [[Sam Gamgee]]'s song of the Stone Troll, unaccompanied and in a "rough and untrained" voice; but as Bratman comments, "but surely so was Sam's." Sayer states in the liner notes of the [[LP album]] of the recordings that Tolkien sang the song to "an old English folk-tune called The Fox and Hens." Bratman states that this is a variant of "The Fox and the Goose" or "[[The Fox (folk song)|The Fox Went Out on a Chilly Night]]".{{efn|The melody can be heard on YouTube.{{cite web |last=Rodgers |first=Jimmie |title=The Fox and the Goose] |date=11 August 2015 |publisher=The Orchard Enterprises |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=exyIRgpQ_Rk}}}} He comments that Tolkien sings in a [[major key]], like [[Cecil Sharp]]'s "southern English melodies" for the song. Bratman finds this "appropriate", noting Tolkien's comment that [[the Shire]] "is in fact more or less a Warwickshire village" of around 1897. In short, Bratman concludes, Tolkien intended readers to imagine Hobbits as "English country folk singing [[English folk music|English folk songs]]."{{cite book |last=Bratman |first=David |author-link=David Bratman |chapter=Liquid Tolkien: Music, Tolkien, Middle-earth, and More Music |editor-last1=Eden |editor-first1=Bradford Lee |editor1-link=Bradford Lee Eden |title=Middle-earth Minstrel: Essays on Music in Tolkien |date=2010 |publisher=[[McFarland & Company|McFarland]] |isbn=978-0-7864-5660-4 |pages=140–170 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AOS74uZTasYC}} The poem appears also in ''[[The Adventures of Tom Bombadil]]''; in the Tolkien critic [[Paul H. Kocher]]'s words, it achieves a certain "grisly slapstick".{{cite book |last=Kocher |first=Paul |author-link=Paul H. Kocher |title=Master of Middle-earth: The Achievement of J.R.R. Tolkien |title-link=Master of Middle-earth |date=1974 |orig-year=1972 |publisher=[[Penguin Books]] |isbn=0140038779 |pages=190–191}} == Adaptations == === Film === [[File:Cave troll.jpg|thumb|right|A cave-troll in [[Peter Jackson]]'s ''The Fellowship of the Ring'']] Trolls are replaced by "Groans" in [[Gene Deitch]]'s [[The Hobbit (1967 film)|1967 animated short film adaptation]] of ''The Hobbit''.{{cite book |last1=Robb |first1=Brian J. |last2=Simpson |first2=Paul |title=Middle-earth Envisioned: The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings: On Screen, On Stage, and Beyond |date=2013 |publisher=[[Race Point Publishing]] |isbn=978-1-93799-427-3 |page=4102 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Nds_AQAAQBAJ&q=groans }} In [[Rankin/Bass]]'s [[The Hobbit (1977 film)|animated 1977 adaptation]] of ''The Hobbit'', the trolls were voiced by [[Paul Frees]], [[Jack DeLeon]], and [[Don Messick]], who all also voiced other characters.{{cite AV media |at=Track A4: The Trolls |title=The Rankin/Bass Production of The Hobbit (The Complete Original Soundtrack) |publisher=[[Buena Vista Records]] |id=103 |type=Vinyl LP |date=1977}} [[Ralph Bakshi]]'s 1978 [[The Lord of the Rings (1978 film)|animated version]] of ''The Lord of the Rings'' follows the book faithfully in its depiction of the encounter with the cave troll in the Chamber, though the cave troll's foot has toes. Glenn Gaslin, reviewing the film on ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]'', describes a clip from the film as "of ravenous trolls, [which] does no justice to Tolkien's darker elements".{{cite web |last=Gaslin |first=Glenn |title=Hobbits on Film |url=https://slate.com/culture/2001/11/ralph-bakshi-s-unfairly-maligned-lord-of-the-rings.html |publisher=[[Slate (website)|Slate]] |access-date=10 April 2020 |date=21 November 2001}} Trolls appear in [[Peter Jackson]]'s [[The Lord of the Rings (film series)|''The Lord of the Rings'' film trilogy]]. In ''[[The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring|The Fellowship of the Ring]]'', [[Bilbo Baggins]] recounts his altercation with the three stone-trolls and later on, the four hobbits and [[Aragorn]] are shown resting in the shelter of the petrified trolls. The location used was Piopio, [[Waitomo District]], in New Zealand.{{cite news |last=Plush |first=Hazel |title=10 epic Middle Earth locations that really exist in New Zealand |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/destinations/oceania/new-zealand/articles/real-life-new-zealand-filming-locations-that-starred-in-the-hobbit-middle-earth/ |access-date=10 April 2020 |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |date=21 September 2017}} In the mines of Moria, a single cave troll, animated in software, is among the attackers and is depicted with two toes.{{cite book |last=Sibley |first=Brian |author-link=Brian Sibley | title=Peter Jackson: A Film-maker's Journey |publisher=[[HarperCollins]] |year=2006 |pages=329–387 |isbn=978-0-00-717558-1 |chapter=Quest for the Ring}}{{cite journal |last=Doyle |first=Audrey |title=The Two Towers |url=https://www.cgw.com/Publications/CGW/2003/Volume-26-Issue-2-Feb-2003-/The-Two-Towers.aspx |journal=Computer Graphics World |volume=26 |issue=2 |access-date=16 April 2020 |pages=n.s |date=February 2003}} [[File:trollaragorn2.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.4|An armoured troll approaches [[Aragorn]] during the [[Battle of the Morannon]] in ''The Return of the King'']] In ''[[The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King|The Return of the King]]'', trolls fight in the [[Battle of the Pelennor Fields]],{{cite web |last=O'Hehir |first=Andrew |title=The Lord of the Rings: Return of the King |url=https://www.salon.com/2003/12/17/return_4/ |work=Salon.com |access-date=16 April 2020 |date=18 December 2003}} and Aragorn fights an armoured troll in the [[Battle of the Morannon]], a departure from the book;{{cite web |last=Evans |first=Willy |title=15 Secrets You Didn't Know Behind The Making Of Lord Of The Rings |url=https://screenrant.com/lord-of-the-rings-bts-secrets/ |website=Screenrant |access-date=16 April 2020 |date=3 March 2018}}{{cite book |last=Leitch |first=Thomas |title=Film Adaptation and Its Discontents: From Gone with the Wind to The Passion of the Christ |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=noLMw2EmFA8C&pg=RA2-PT57 |year=2009 |publisher=[[Johns Hopkins University Press]] |isbn=978-0-8018-9187-8 |page=2}} Jackson had at one stage intended Aragorn to fight the Dark Lord Sauron in person, but "wisely" reduced this to combat with a troll.{{cite book |last=Rateliff |first=John D. |author-link=John D. Rateliff |chapter=Two Kinds of Absence |editor-last1=Bogstad |editor-first1=Janice M. |editor-last2=Kaveny |editor-first2=Philip E. |title=[[Picturing Tolkien]] |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jNjKrXRP0G8C&pg=PA66 |year=2011 |publisher=[[McFarland & Company|McFarland]] |isbn=978-0-7864-8473-7 |pages=65–66 |url-status=live |archive-date=2023-05-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230528054813/https://books.google.at/books?id=jNjKrXRP0G8C&pg=PA66&redir_esc=y}} [[File:Trolls from The Hobbit in Te Papa (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|Stone trolls as they appear in ''[[The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey]]'', at [[Te Papa]].]] In ''[[The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey]]'' the three stone trolls appear as in Tolkien's book. The trolls are portrayed through voice and [[motion capture]] with Bert performed by [[Mark Hadlow]], Tom is performed by [[William Kircher]], and William is performed by [[Peter Hambleton]].{{cite web |title=The Hobbit Then and Now |url=https://www.insider.com/the-hobbit-then-and-now-2018-12 |publisher=The Insider |access-date=10 April 2020 |date=2 January 2019}} In ''[[The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies]]'', trolls appear in Azog's army as shock troops. Some of the trolls have catapults mounted on their backs while others have bladed shields and other strange weaponry, such as one troll who had flails sutured to its limbs. Behind the scenes, Peter Jackson's design team added trolls to the orc army, saying that they were a "natural extension of the orcs' forces".{{cite web |last=Gilsdorf |first=Ethan |title=Peter Jackson Must Be Stopped |url=https://www.wired.com/2014/12/hobbit-peter-jackson-must-be-stopped/ |publisher=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] |access-date=10 April 2020 |date=19 December 2014}}{{cite book |last=Falconer |first=Daniel |title=The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies Chronicles: Art and Design |date=2014 |publisher=[[Harper Design]] |location=New York |isbn=978-0-06226-571-5 |pages=217–221}} === Television === The trolls appear in the [[Amazon Studios]] series ''[[The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power]]''. The first episode of [[The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 1|season one]] featured a snow-troll that attacked Galadriel's group at the abandoned fortress at Forodwaith. She was able to slay the snow-troll.{{Cite web |last=Hogg |first=Trevor |date=October 30, 2022 |title='The Rings of Power': The VFX of a Dazzling Return to Middle-earth |url=https://www.animationmagazine.net/2022/10/the-rings-of-power-the-vfx-of-a-dazzling-return-to-middle-earth/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221031024449/https://www.animationmagazine.net/2022/10/the-rings-of-power-the-vfx-of-a-dazzling-return-to-middle-earth/ |archive-date=October 31, 2022 |access-date=March 1, 2023 |website=[[Animation Magazine]]}} [[The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 2|Season two]] features a hill-troll named Damrod (voiced by [[Benjamin Walker (actor)|Benjamin Walker]] in "[[The Eagle and the Sceptre]]",{{Cite web |last=Travis |first=Ben |date=January 7, 2024 |title=Meet The Rings Of Power's New Hill-Troll, Inspired By Breaking Bad's Mike Ehrmantraut – Exclusive Image |url=https://www.empireonline.com/tv/news/rings-of-power-season-2-hill-troll-breaking-bad-mike-ehrmantraut/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240701142509/https://www.empireonline.com/tv/news/rings-of-power-season-2-hill-troll-breaking-bad-mike-ehrmantraut/ |archive-date=July 1, 2024 |access-date=July 1, 2024 |website=[[Empire (magazine)|Empire]]}} [[Jason Smith (visual effects)|Jason Smith]] in "[[Doomed to Die (The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power)|Doomed to Die]]"{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Ralph |date=August 28, 2024 |title='It was bloody hard work': what it's like to be a 16ft TV troll |url=https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/article/2024/aug/28/rings-of-power-troll-how-actors-portray-tvs-great-fantasy-monsters |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240828142101/https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/article/2024/aug/28/rings-of-power-troll-how-actors-portray-tvs-great-fantasy-monsters |archive-date=August 28, 2024 |access-date=September 28, 2024 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}) who allies with Adar's forces. Damrod is described by Adar to be the "Eater of Dragon Bones" and "Slayer of the Stone Giants". After bringing back the head of an orc messenger sent to persuade him to ally with Adar, Damrod asks "Where is Sauron"?{{cite magazine |last=Murray |first=Emily |title=One Rings of Power actor pulls double duty in surprising fashion - with this unrecognizable season 2 voice role |magazine=Games Radar |date=29 August 2024 |url=https://www.gamesradar.com/entertainment/lord-of-the-rings-tv-shows/rings-of-power-damrod-actor-explained/ |access-date=3 September 2024}} === Games === Trolls have featured in many [[Middle-earth in video games|video games set in Middle-earth]], including ''[[The Lord of the Rings: The Battle for Middle-earth]]'',{{cite web |last=IGN Staff |title=Battle for Middle-Earth - Mordor, Part 2 |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/11/12/battle-for-middle-earth-mordor-part-2 |publisher=IGN |access-date=19 April 2020 |date=12 November 2004}} ''[[The Lord of the Rings: The Battle for Middle-earth II]]'', ''[[The Lord of the Rings: The Third Age]]'',{{cite web |last=IGN Staff |title=The Third Age: Forces of Evil |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/10/21/the-third-age-forces-of-evil |publisher=IGN |access-date=19 April 2020 |date=21 October 2004}} and ''[[The Lord of the Rings: Conquest]]''.{{cite web |last=McCarthy |first=Dave |title=Lord of the Rings Conquest UK Review |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2009/01/16/lord-of-the-rings-conquest-uk-review |publisher=IGN |access-date=19 April 2020 |date=16 January 2009}} In ''[[The Lord of the Rings: The Battle for Middle-earth II: The Rise of the Witch-king]]'', the Angmar faction has a hill-troll hero named Rogash (voiced by [[Gregg Berger]]),{{cite web |last=Barratt |first=Charlie |title=LOTR: The Battle for Middle-earth II: The Rise of the Witch-king |url=https://www.gamesradar.com/uk/lotr-the-battle-for-middle-earth-ii-the-rise-of-the-witch-king/2/ |publisher=GamesRadar |access-date=19 April 2020 |date=23 August 2006}}{{cite web |last=Adams |first=Dan |title=The Rise of the Witch-king Hands-on |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2006/11/04/the-rise-of-the-witch-king-hands-on |publisher=IGN |access-date=19 April 2020 |date=4 November 2006}} and an Olog-hai named Brûz the Chopper (voiced by [[Gideon Emery]]) is important to the plot of ''[[Middle-earth: Shadow of War]]''.{{cite web |last=Graeber |first=Brendan |title=Shadow of War's Nemesis System Took Things Way Too Far |url=https://in.ign.com/shadow-of-mordor-2/133245/news/shadow-of-wars-nemesis-system-took-things-way-too-far |publisher=IGN India |access-date=19 April 2020 |date=15 March 2019}} Middle-earth trolls have appeared in [[List of Middle-earth role-playing games|tabletop role-playing games]]; for example, the core book for ''[[Middle-earth Role Playing]]'', published by [[Iron Crown Enterprises]], included rules for Normal Trolls, Olog-hai (or Black Trolls), and Half-Trolls,{{Cite book |last1=Charlton |first1=S. Coleman |last2=Ruemmler |first2=John D. |title=Middle-earth Role Playing |url=https://archive.org/details/middleearthrolep00char |url-access=limited |year=1986 |publisher=Ice Crown Enterprises |pages=[https://archive.org/details/middleearthrolep00char/page/n17 17]-18 |isbn=978-0915795314}} and the publisher released an [[adventure module]] called ''[[Trolls of the Misty Mountains]]''.{{cite book |last1=Cresswell |first1=John |last2=Cresswell |first2=Mike |year=1986 |title=[[Trolls of the Misty Mountains]] |publisher=Iron Crown Enterprises |isbn=978-0915795499}} ''[[Middle Earth Strategy Battle Game]]'' includes trolls, while [[Games Workshop]] produce a selection of troll miniatures.{{cite web |url=https://www.games-workshop.com/en-GB/Mordor-Troll-Chieftain |title=Mordor Troll Chieftain |publisher=Games Workshop |access-date=18 April 2019}}{{cite web |url=https://www.games-workshop.com/en-GB/Cave-Troll |title=Cave Troll |publisher=Games Workshop |access-date=18 April 2019}}{{cite web |url=https://www.games-workshop.com/en-GB/Mordor-Troll-2018 |title=Mordor Troll |publisher=Games Workshop |access-date=18 April 2019}}{{cite web |url=https://www.games-workshop.com/en-GB/Half-Trolls |title=Half Trolls |publisher=Games Workshop |access-date=18 April 2019}}{{cite web |url=https://www.games-workshop.com/en-GB/Hill-Troll-Chieftain-Buhrdur |title=Hill Troll Chieftain Buhrdur |publisher=Games Workshop |access-date=18 April 2019}} == Notes == {{notelist}} == References == === Primary === {{reflist|group=T|28em}} === Secondary === {{reflist|28em}} === Sources === * {{ME-ref|Letters}} * {{ME-ref|TH}} * {{ME-ref|FOTR}} * {{ME-ref|TT}} * {{ME-ref|ROTK}} * {{ME-ref|Silm}} * {{ME-ref|Children of Hurin}} {{Middle-earth}} {{Hobbit}} {{Lotr}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Troll (Middle-earth)}} [[Category:Fictional trolls]] [[Category:Middle-earth races]] [[Category:Middle-earth monsters]]
